Mark Cuban on Why AI Could Turn Solo Founders Into Trillionaires60 min41 insights2026-10-28
▶ Watch on YouTube
Despite the title, most of this conversation is Mark Cuban on healthcare economics: how Cost Plus Drugs (now ~4,000 SKUs), its Dallas manufacturing and ~$20M tractor-trailer drug-manufacturing 'pods', Cost Plus Marketplace and direct hospital contracting attack vertically integrated insurers (BUAs) like UnitedHealth that profit from opaque ASO contracts and spread pricing. Cuban argues the fastest cost lever is employers running benefit contracts through AI before signing, proposes transparency mandates and a bank-plus-stop-loss alternative to insurance, and only briefly touches the 'trillionaire in the basement' solo-founder idea and AI-industry marketing.

Why AI Could Turn Small Law Firms Into Billion-Dollar Businesses52 min22 insights2026-10-30
▶ Watch on YouTube
a16z's Alex Rampell interviews Jay, co-founder and CEO of portfolio company Eve, about AI for plaintiff (contingency) law. Their argument is that the sector is limited by labor rather than demand, so AI expands firm revenue (one LA firm went from 100 to 500 clients per attorney), settlement data that cannot be scraped forms a moat, and outcome-based pricing and law-firm consolidation will spread.

Plaintiff law is supply-constrained 6
Plaintiff (contingency) law is limited by the supply of legal labor, not by demand: firms turn away most inbound leads because working each case costs more than the fee it would earn.
thesis🗣 Jay (Eve co-founder & CEO)conviction: highEveplaintiff law
So what: AI that lowers the cost of legal labor opens up a market that was previously uneconomic.
Plaintiff firms typically will not take a case unless it yields at least about $5,000 in fees, and even at that level many cases lose money; firms count on a few large payouts.
data_point🗣 Jay (Eve co-founder & CEO)conviction: highplaintiff law
So what: Small-damage cases, such as fender-benders below the deductible, go entirely unrepresented today.
“Today, if a lawyer doesn't make at least 5,000 fees of a case, they do not take it on.” ▶ 6:31
About 96% of labor and employment cases are rejected, because screening one costs roughly 30-45 minutes of intake plus about 10 hours of research to tie the facts to a cause of action.
data_point🗣 Jay (Eve co-founder & CEO)conviction: mediumEEOC
So what: Automating intake and legal research changes the economics of an entire category of law.
“So that is why 96% of cases on the labor unemployment side, for example, gets rejected” ▶ 8:27
On a typical $25,000 settlement the attorney takes about a third (about $8,000), of which roughly half goes to labor, about 30% to marketing, and the rest is profit, leaving little to reinvest.
data_point🗣 Jay (Eve co-founder & CEO)conviction: mediumplaintiff law
So what: If AI removes much of the labor share, firm margins and reinvestment capacity rise sharply.
VCs underestimated plaintiff-law software because existing spend was tiny (a phone, email, sometimes not even Microsoft Word), when the real opportunity is the 'shadow labor market' behind hundreds of billions of dollars a year in outcomes.
contrarian🗣 Alex Rampell (a16z)conviction: highMicrosoft WordMicrosoft OfficeHarvey
So what: Legal AI should be sized against labor spend and outcomes, not against legacy software budgets.
“the software market is kind of like this shadow labor market” ▶ 17:11
Most legal software money, including Harvey's, has gone to the defense and institutional side because that is where the budgets are, leaving plaintiff firms underserved.
causal🗣 Jay (Eve co-founder & CEO)conviction: mediumHarvey
So what: Plaintiff law is a less contested niche for vertical legal AI.

Proprietary data moat vs. foundation models 3
Less than about 1% of plaintiff cases become published opinions, because most settle before a demand or before litigation, so the most valuable settlement data cannot be scraped by foundation models.

So what: Vertical apps with exclusive outcome data can defend against general-purpose labs.

Insurers like Geico and State Farm see outcomes across thousands of firms (and use valuation software like Colossus), while plaintiff firms are fragmented; pooled tactics data on Eve narrows that information gap, but Eve does not train on privileged client data.
framework🗣 Jay (Eve co-founder & CEO)conviction: mediumGeicoState FarmColossusEve

A frontier model dropped into a law firm, like 'Albert Einstein', would not be productive at first; Eve's value is the local context (jurisdiction, opposing counsel, insurer tactics) that sits on top of better models.
framework🗣 Jay (Eve co-founder & CEO)conviction: mediumEve

Lawfare Daily: FCC’s Bad Labs Rulemaking with FCC’s Andy Hendrickson and Alice Jou40 min18 insights2026-10-28

FCC Office of Engineering and Technology officials Andy Hendrickson and Alice Jou explain how US RF-device testing migrated to China (US share of applications by testing-firm location fell from ~31% in 2007 to under 4% in 2025 while China rose from ~15% to ~82%), detail the Derrycom case (a Chinese-owned certification body posing as Minnesota-based that became the #4 TCB within 18 months), and lay out the 'bad labs' / equipment authorization integrity agenda culminating in a proposal to stop recognizing labs in non-reciprocal economies from December 1, 2028.

FCC equipment authorization data show the US share of applications by testing-firm location fell from about 31% in 2007 to below 4% in 2025, while the share tied to testing firms in China rose from about 15% to roughly 82%.

The migration of device testing to China was driven by manufacturing relocation plus an FCC policy shift that prioritized accreditation/technical competence over reciprocity, letting foreign labs serve the US market while US labs lacked equal access abroad.

So what: Regulatory design, not just labor cost, created the dependency, so regulatory reversal can partially undo it.

Derrycom, a certification body registered at a small Minnesota address and approved in October 2024, became the #4 of 40 FCC certification bodies within 18 months, certifying almost 12,000 applications, and was the #2 body in Canada's market.

The FCC frames its equipment authorization integrity proceeding as three steps: a 2025 action barring labs/TCBs/accreditors owned or controlled by prohibited entities, an April 2026 action fast-tracking devices tested in trusted (US or reciprocal) labs, and a pending vote to stop recognizing labs in non-reciprocal economies.

Recorded October 22, Commodity Context's Rory Johnston updates Nate Hagens on the eighth month of the Iran war: non-Iranian Gulf crude exports briefly recovered to pre-war levels in late September before Iran's heaviest attacks of the war, but freight is $20-30/bbl (10x normal), more than 2 billion barrels of Middle East output has been lost, and refined products, especially diesel (cracks around 5-6x normal, New York Harbor diesel futures at $227/bbl), are the real crisis. In a solo episode, Nate Hagens argues that GDP growth is a biophysical anomaly funded by debt claims that have outrun the net energy surplus (the 'Wile E. Coyote gap'). He lays out seven ways growth ends, with 'biophysical musical chairs' as his main bet, and points to France's 10-year yield breaking 5%, US debt growth, a record-low SPR and the debt-funded, energy-constrained AI build-out as live warning signs.

Growth as a biophysical anomaly 5
Hagens argues that GDP is essentially a tally of energy and materials pulled through the economy, and that technology has never anywhere let the economy grow while physical throughput stayed flat.
thesis🗣 Nate Hagensconviction: highGDP
So what: Growth forecasts that assume decoupling from resources are, in his view, unfounded.
Historically, materials use and GDP are correlated about one-for-one and energy about 0.7; 3% annual growth means GDP doubles about every 23 years, so in 70 years GDP would be 8x larger, requiring more than 4x the energy and about 800 billion tons of material a year versus today's 100.
data_point🗣 Nate Hagensconviction: highGDP
So what: The 3% perpetual-growth assumption in government and pension plans conflicts with physical constraints.
Hagens says every government and pension fund assumes roughly 3% annual growth in perpetuity, which he believes the physical base cannot support.
contrarian🗣 Nate Hagensconviction: highpension funds
So what: Long-dated liabilities priced on perpetual growth are at risk.
Money is the proximate driver of the economy and energy applied to materials is the ultimate driver; as the cheapest oil and richest ores were depleted, society 'printed more claims' against a shrinking surplus, which delayed the feedback from physical limits.
causal🗣 Nate Hagensconviction: highdebt
So what: Financial claims have outgrown the real resource base, so a reconciliation is coming.

Inside the $6 Billion Binance Hack31 min19 insights2026-10-30
▶ Watch on YouTube
TRM Labs' Ari Redbord, interviewed hours after a roughly $6 billion Binance hot-wallet hack attributed to North Korea, says Tether and Circle froze about 40% (~$2.4B) of the stolen funds within about an hour, the largest recovery ever, yet the net theft is still about 2x Bybit's $1.5B record. He describes the staging/rehearsal signature, the Beacon Network response, the GENIUS Act freeze provisions being validated, AI as an escalating threat, and the case for offensive and diplomatic pressure (via China) on North Korea.

Scale and attribution of the Binance hack 5
The Binance hack totaled roughly $6 billion, which Ari Redbord calls the largest bank robbery in human history, compared with the previous record $1.5 billion Bybit hack.
data_point🗣 Ari Redbordconviction: highBinanceBybitNorth Korea
So what: Exchange custody tail risk is now an order of magnitude larger than assumed.
“this is the largest bank robbery in human history” ▶ 4:32
Redbord says North Korea has stolen about $6-8 billion in crypto over the last six years and then stole about $6 billion in a single evening from Binance.
data_point🗣 Ari Redbordconviction: highNorth KoreaBinance
So what: State-actor theft capacity is accelerating sharply.
With North Korea's economy estimated at around $20 billion, the $6 billion theft equals roughly a third of its entire economy, making it a global security issue tied to nuclear weapons ambitions.
data_point🗣 Ari Redbordconviction: highNorth Korea
So what: Raises odds of national-security-level policy responses toward crypto.
TRM attributed the hack to North Korea partly via its staging-and-rehearsal signature: small Tornado Cash withdrawals at least 36 hours before, attack code tested on two wallets and rehearsed on a third with test funds routed back, then installed on the Binance hot wallet, plus address links to the Drift and Bybit hacks.
data_point🗣 Ari Redbordconviction: highTornado CashBinanceDriftBybitNorth Korea
So what: Pre-attack on-chain staging is detectable in hindsight but hard to flag in real time.
Binance's account that an engineer's laptop or computer systems were compromised to gain access to private keys is consistent with what TRM saw on-chain, pointing to social engineering.
causal🗣 Ari Redbordconviction: mediumBinance
So what: Operational security of key holders, not smart-contract bugs, is the weak point.

Tether and Circle froze about 40% of the stolen funds, roughly $2.4 billion, within about an hour of the hack, which Redbord says is more than has been recovered in any hack ever.
data_point🗣 Ari Redbordconviction: highTetherCircle
So what: Issuer freeze capability materially reduces loss severity for stablecoin holdings.

TRM's Beacon Network, an information-sharing network covering about 85% of centralized crypto volume (including Binance, Coinbase, Kraken, OKX, Robinhood, Stripe, PayPal) and about 100 law enforcement agencies, coordinated real-time flagging of illicit addresses during the hack.

If UPI Is Free, Who Pays for It? | PhonePe, Razorpay & NPCI | WTF is Payments?240 min49 insights2026-10-30
▶ Watch on YouTube
Four-and-a-half-hour roundtable with Nikhil Kamath, PhonePe CEO Sameer Nigam, Razorpay co-founder Harshil Mathur and NPCI growth ED Sohini dissecting UPI and card economics (who pays the ~25 bps UPI cost, the 1.85% card MDR stack), the zero-MDR and 30% market-cap fights, and India's over-regulation problem. It closes with views on CBDCs vs stablecoins, agentic payments (NPCI planning agentic UPI), the AI bubble, and Kamath's contrarian buys (Infosys/IT services, hotels, BookMyShow, energy storage), plus short cross-border/wearable founder segments.
UPI plumbing and who pays for 'free' · 8Card and online merchant economics · 7Zero MDR, market-share caps and fear of big · 10Consumption data and the shape of Indian demand · 7B2B, cross-border, stablecoins and CBDCs · 7Agentic commerce, AI bubble and contrarian bets · 10
UPI plumbing and who pays for 'free' 8
UPI processes roughly 783 million transactions a day (close to a billion including everything), and NPCI, a not-for-profit Section 8 company seeded with Rs 100 crore by ten banks, has self-funded all growth from surplus without paying dividends to its bank and fintech shareholders.
data_point🗣 Sohini (NPCI)conviction: highNPCIUPI
So what: UPI's core rail is a non-profit utility, so private monetisation has to come from apps, PSP banks and MDR rather than the switch.
“Yes, so 783 million yesterday.” ▶ 47:16
A single P2P UPI transfer involves roughly seven actors (app/TPAP, PSP sponsor bank, NPCI, issuer bank, beneficiary bank, VPA resolution) and about 10 API calls, at an estimated ecosystem-wide cost of about 25 basis points.
data_point🗣 Sameer Nigam / Sohiniconviction: mediumUPINPCIPhonePe
So what: 'Free' UPI has a real cost borne by banks and apps, which is the economic basis for the MDR debate.
“So, each transaction is roughly 10 API calls.” ▶ 58:54
On a P2P UPI transfer the remitter's issuing bank pays the app's PSP bank a slab-based fee of roughly 15 to 50 paise, which PhonePe shares, justified as a saving versus branch, ATM and NEFT servicing costs (NEFT also costs banks 50 paise).
data_point🗣 Sameer Nigamconviction: mediumPhonePeCanara BankYes BankAxis BankNEFT
So what: PSP-bank fees are the thin existing revenue line for UPI apps absent MDR.
PhonePe runs about 30,000 servers, claims the second-largest data footprint in India after the Jio group, and employs roughly 1,500-1,800 engineers on fraud, risk and settlement for UPI.
data_point🗣 Sameer Nigamconviction: highPhonePeJio
So what: Running a top UPI app is capital- and engineering-intensive despite zero consumer pricing.
“We have about 30,000 servers now.” ▶ 1:02:56
NPCI settles UPI ten times a day on a net basis through RTGS accounts at RBI, so 100 million peak-hour transactions collapse into roughly 800 gross settlement entries, and no intermediary holds float as in wallet-based Alipay/WeChat.
framework🗣 Sohini (NPCI) / Sameer Nigamconviction: highNPCIRBIAlipayWeChat
So what: Ledger-based real-time payments with deferred net settlement is why UPI scales cheaply, but also why there is no float income for apps.
“We settle ten times a day.” ▶ 1:06:24
The regulator backed UPI because Nandan Nilekani's camp warned that if India went digital on cards, Visa and Mastercard would take a monopoly worth about 50 basis points of GDP; the core build team was only about 20 people (Nilekani, Sharad Sharma, Pramod Jain, Sanjay Gupta, Dilip Asbe and others).
anecdote🗣 Sameer Nigamconviction: highNandan NilekaniVisaMastercardISPIRTNPCI
So what: UPI was a sovereign-rails decision, which explains policy hostility to card-network economics.
“Visa and Mastercard will have a monopoly on and 50 basis points of the GDP.” ▶ 48:40
UPI's monthly volume runs about Rs 29.33 lakh crore (about a lakh crore a day), meaning annual UPI TPV now exceeds one turn of GDP, while retail B2C payments are typically only 1.2-1.3x GDP, so UPI is close to capturing most retail spending.
data_point🗣 Sameer Nigamconviction: mediumUPIRBI
So what: Remaining UPI growth must come from B2B, government and larger-ticket flows rather than retail substitution.
RBI estimates 60% of household consumption spending is still cash (versus 80% three years earlier), whereas in the pre-UPI cards era only about 3% of personal consumption expenditure was digital.
data_point🗣 Nikhil Kamath / Sohini (NPCI)conviction: mediumRBIUPI
So what: Digital share of consumption has inflected sharply but large cash pools (rent, property, B2B) remain.
Card and online merchant economics 7
On a credit-card transaction Razorpay charges a large merchant like Amazon about 1.85%, pays about 1.75% downstream and keeps about 10 bps, with roughly 1.45% going to the issuing bank to fund cost of credit and rewards; Visa/Mastercard take far less than the commonly assumed 2%.
data_point🗣 Harshil Mathurconviction: highRazorpayAmazonVisaMastercardRuPay
So what: Payment-gateway margins are razor thin; the issuer, not the network, captures most of the MDR.
“So, I'll make 10 basis points.” ▶ 1:46:06
Payment gateways price ad valorem rather than flat because they underwrite merchant-default risk: if a merchant takes payments and disappears, the acquirer/aggregator is liable for chargebacks.
framework🗣 Harshil Mathurconviction: highRazorpay
So what: Merchant underwriting is the real moat and cost centre of PGs, not the switching.
“The percentage based is because I am essentially underwriting a risk.” ▶ 1:53:13
For online merchants cash-on-delivery costs about 5% once fraud, logistics and returns are counted, which is higher than a 1.75% card MDR, so charging MDR on online UPI would not push merchants back to cash.
causal🗣 Harshil Mathurconviction: highAmazonFlipkart
So what: The online MDR case differs from offline kiranas; policy should segment by use case.
≈ “COD is 5%.” paraphrase
The US has high card success rates but 100-200 bps fraud because it lacks two-factor authentication, while India's mandated 2FA/OTP crushed consumer-side fraud but raised failure rates; Razorpay's edge was engineering higher success rates across the chain.
framework🗣 Harshil Mathurconviction: highRazorpay
So what: In India, payment success rate is the key competitive metric for online gateways.
During Flipkart's first Big Billion Day sale, about 10 million card payment attempts in eight hours saw roughly 9 million fail, core banking systems of several banks including SBI went down, and 35,000-40,000 TVs were sold on 'failed' transactions later deemed successful.
anecdote🗣 Sameer Nigamconviction: highFlipkartSBIHDFCVisaMastercard
So what: Legacy card and bank stacks were not built for Indian peak scale, which created the opening for UPI.
“I remember we drove about 10 million credit card and debit card payment attempts in a eight-hour window, 9 million of them failed.” ▶ 45:34
Urban Indians under 30 average two credit cards, and the majority of those are RuPay cards because RuPay credit works on UPI QR acceptance, which Visa and Mastercard cards cannot.
data_point🗣 Harshil Mathur / Sohini (NPCI)conviction: mediumRuPayUPIVisaMastercard

“majority of those cards under 30 are actually RuPay cards today” ▶ 1:50:01
Acquirer-side price cuts do not drive card usage because consumers choose the instrument; issuers instead pass margin back as cashback and reward multipliers, often co-funded with platforms during sales.

Chat With Traders 1 episode(s) · 39 insights

Why Your Trading Strategy Might Be Wrong for You · Alex Temiz and Bao Nguyen91 min39 insights2026-10-28

Live Chat With Traders panel in Orlando with MIC founders Alex Temiz and Bao Nguyen on trading process: exponential setup-graded sizing (C/B/A = 1k/5k/20k shares), pre-planned entry/exit/stop/target, broker-enforced max loss, and small-cap red-flag checklists. They note the post-PDT market has become more irrational, adding to winners is not currently rewarded, and the 'first red day' now requires a break of the prior day's low.
Exponential bet sizing by setup grade · 9Pre-planning, stops and risk controls · 9Stock selection and red flags · 7Market regime changes: post-PDT and evolving setups · 6Personal style, account management and psychology · 8
Exponential bet sizing by setup grade 9
Alex Temiz says that using identical size on every setup produced swings of +$10k/-$20k/+$30k/-$20k/+$50k/-$40k and a break-even week; grading setups fixed the inconsistency.
anecdote🗣 Alex Temizconviction: high
So what: Uniform sizing across setups of different quality destroys edge; size must scale with probability.
“I was up 10,000 one day, down 20,000 the next day. Up 30,000, down 20,000, up 50,000 minus 40,000. And at the end of the week, somehow I was break even” ▶ 0:02
Temiz's exponential sizing framework uses roughly 1,000 shares on a C setup, 5,000 on a B setup and 20,000 on an A setup, a 20x difference between C and A grades.
framework🗣 Alex Temizconviction: high
So what: Grade-based share size should differ by an order of magnitude, not by small increments.
“on a C setup, let's use a,000 shares. On a B setup, you use 5,000 shares. On A setup, you use 20,000 shares.” ▶ 1:26:02
Temiz argues that on a true, back-tested A setup, dollar risk should be at least 5-10x normal daily risk (e.g., $100 normal to $500-$1,000), not merely doubled to $200.
framework🗣 Alex Temizconviction: high
So what: Traders who only double risk on best setups leave most of the edge on the table.
Bao Nguyen cautions beginners not to jump straight to sizing multiples; size should ramp gradually after back-testing and building trust in a setup, because Alex's A setup may be someone else's worst setup.
contrarian🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: highAlex Temiz
So what: Copying a mentor's size without your own data on the setup is a path to large losses.
“If you do not know what your best setup is, you have not earned the ability to size up.” ▶ 1:29:02
Temiz frames setup quality with a 'Bao at Disney World (50%) vs Bao at the club (99%)' analogy: bet heavy only on near-certain setups and light on coin-flips.
framework🗣 Alex Temizconviction: mediumBao Nguyen
So what: Explicit probability estimation per setup is the precondition for variable sizing.
Nguyen compares trading to blackjack where you can see your cards before betting: wait for 18-20 hands, start with a small bet and add only on confirmation, and never go all in because 20 still loses to 21.
framework🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: high
So what: Trading's key advantage over casino games is discretionary bet timing and scaling into winners.
“Unlike a blackjack, blackjack makes you forced to bet blind, right? You're not betting blind, guys.” ▶ 0:14
Temiz observes that across 250 trading days, maximum aggression is warranted only once or twice a year, yet most traders are aggressive on 248 days and timid on the two that matter.
contrarian🗣 Alex Temizconviction: high
So what: Most retail P&L damage comes from over-aggression on ordinary days.
“There's 250 trading days in the year. 248 of them, you should really probably not be that aggressive.” ▶ 11:22
Temiz says the biggest barrier for most traders is size rather than strategy: if you can't succeed with 50 shares you won't with 1,000-10,000, and cutting size in half would make most traders successful.
thesis🗣 Alex Temizconviction: high
So what: Size reduction is the highest-ROI fix for struggling traders.
“if you cannot be successful with 50 shares, you will never be successful with a,000 shares, 5,000 shares, 10,000 shares.” ▶ 10:58
Temiz's scaling method: take a 10-15% starter; add only on confirmation signals (for shorts: break under VWAP, a 'death candle', low-of-day break) and exit on invalidation (VWAP reclaim, death-candle reclaim, high-of-day break), with win odds rising roughly 50% to 75% to 90% as signals stack.
framework🗣 Alex Temizconviction: highVWAP
So what: Confirmation-based adds let traders be aggressive without front-loading risk.
Pre-planning, stops and risk controls 9
Temiz, citing coaching from Dr. Brett Steenbarger, says nervousness in a trade means one of four things is unplanned: entry, exit, stop or target; he wrote all four on a post-it note per watch-list stock.
framework🗣 Alex Temizconviction: highBrett Steenbarger
So what: A written four-point plan per ticker before the open removes in-trade emotional decision making.
“that means that you have not planned one of four things. Your entry, your exit, your stop, or your target.” ▶ 1:03
Nguyen trades with pre-placed limit 'fantasy orders' and argues fear comes from the unknown; knowing maximum loss in advance via math eliminates fear, and if scared you should size down.
framework🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: high
So what: Pre-committed orders convert discretionary trading into execution of a plan.
“I already put out my orders. I call them fantasy orders.” ▶ 1:07
Nguyen says the trade-off is mechanical: smaller size with a wider range produces the same dollar outcome as big size with a tight range, and most traders do better small and capturing more of the move.
framework🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: high
So what: Wider stops with smaller size reduce noise stop-outs without raising dollar risk.
Nguyen's rule of thumb: to make 10 cents you need a 20-cent range, and Temiz adds that on a stock with a $1 range a stop should be ~50 cents, not 10 cents.
framework🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: high
So what: Target and stop distances must be scaled to the instrument's range to avoid being shaken out.
“if you want 10 cents you need a 20 cent range” ▶ 1:09:15
Nguyen dismisses stop-hunting fears for small accounts but says he avoids round-number stops (e.g., uses $2.14 rather than $2.00) because herd stops cluster there.

Nguyen insists on broker-level max loss and per-ticker auto-liquidation (via Cobra) and says premarket has no auto-liquidation, so premarket trading carries uncapped risk.
thesis🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: highCobra
So what: Hard broker-enforced loss caps are the only reliable defense against blow-ups.
“If you're trading premarket, there's no auto liquidation premarket.” ▶ 33:41

framework🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: medium
So what: Reward-distance check before entry filters out poor risk/reward trades.
Stock selection and red flags 7
Temiz narrows ~17,000 moving stocks to about four on his daily watch list and says members who trade off-list (e.g., going long silver on the day he made $100k shorting gold) consistently lose.
anecdote🗣 Alex Temizconviction: highgoldsilver
So what: Disciplined universe restriction is itself an edge.
Temiz's red-flag list for small-cap trades: float under 1 million shares, Chinese stocks, ADRs, SSR on, day-one runners, high short float, high institutional ownership, and press releases signalling serial pivots (AI to crypto to marijuana).
framework🗣 Alex Temizconviction: high
So what: A checklist of disqualifiers prevents trading structurally dangerous tickers.
“number one is low float, less than 1 million share float. Chinese stocks have been very, very risky. ADR stocks have been very, very risky.” ▶ 45:00
Temiz argues shorting a hyped stock on day one is like fighting a young Mike Tyson; day two, when hype fades, offers better odds and sometimes clean 50% fades with no bounces.
thesis🗣 Alex Temizconviction: high
So what: For momentum shorts, waiting for day two trades off some upside for much better odds.
“You don't want to be fighting Mike Tyson from 20 years ago, but day two is Mike Tyson that fought Jake Paul.” ▶ 56:50
Temiz and Nguyen say they trade 9:30-10:30 and that members who keep trading 'random' names after 10:30 give back morning gains; the less you trade, the more you often make.
thesis🗣 Alex Temizconviction: high
So what: Restricting trading to the highest-volume window improves expectancy.
“Oftentimes, the less you trade, the more money you make” ▶ 18:01
Nguyen uses AI prompts to replace manual due diligence on small caps: 'why did this stock go up today?', 'is there dilution?', and 'are there upcoming events?', cutting research that took ages to about 30 seconds.
data_point🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: high
So what: LLM-assisted dilution/catalyst checks are becoming a standard retail day-trading edge.
“Holy crap, that used to take us forever, dude. Now it's like a 30 seconds.” ▶ 46:45
Nguyen predicts AI will replace back-room due-diligence finance analysts.
prediction🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: medium
So what: Junior research roles in finance face displacement by LLM tooling.

Nguyen says he avoids shorting stocks running ahead of a known event like an investor conference next week, preferring to short on the event day (buy the rumor, sell the news).
framework🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: medium
So what: Catalyst calendars matter for timing short entries in small caps.
Market regime changes: post-PDT and evolving setups 6
Temiz says since the PDT rule went away, small-cap moves have become more irrational and crazier due to many more market participants.
causal🗣 Alex Temizconviction: highPDT
So what: Removal of the pattern-day-trader rule has increased retail-driven volatility in small caps.
“ever since PDT went away, a lot of these moves are way more irrational” ▶ 57:41
Temiz says adding to winners currently isn't rewarded because stocks keep reclaiming, so he has shifted to 'nail and bail' singles, whereas six months ago adding to winners massively improved P&L.
thesis🗣 Alex Temizconviction: high
So what: Strategy must adapt to regime: in the current cycle, take profits quickly.
“right now, adding to a winner is not rewarding.” ▶ 58:34
Temiz says the 'first red day' setup has evolved: it now requires the stock to both go red and break below the previous day's low, as seen on CAR (Avis) this year.
framework🗣 Alex Temizconviction: highCAR
So what: Classic setups decay; adding a prior-day-low break filter restores the first-red-day edge.
“The new trick is not only does it have to go red, it has to go under the previous day's lows.” ▶ 52:13
Nguyen says small caps are no longer all-day faders and can reclaim to much higher levels, so he scalps ~20 cents on dollar stocks (20%) rather than holding for the backside, and the 'low-hanging fruit' day-two continuation short has periodically stopped working.
thesis🗣 Bao Nguyenconviction: medium

Temiz cites silver, gold, oil and CAR as the big trading opportunities of this year.
data_point🗣 Alex Temizconviction: mediumsilvergoldoilCAR
So what: Macro commodity moves have been a major day-trading opportunity set in 2026.

Temiz and Nguyen trade the same stocks at similar levels but very differently: Nguyen runs ~10-20 names with quick partials and adds liquidity, while Temiz focuses on one stock with full attention and removes liquidity on winners.

RAND Center for the Geopolitics of AGI researchers Joel Predd, Ben Boudreaux and Matt Chessen walk Nathan Labenz through their 'Maintaining Freedom of Action' paper: seven archetypal superintelligence strategies (acceleration, dominance, co-development, preparedness, moratorium, deterrence, continuity of society), five pivot questions that select among them, and the argument that the US should now build no-regret, long-lead capabilities (verification, compute visibility, evals, incident response, secure data centers) from a 106-item security architecture catalog rather than commit prematurely. Seven archetypes and five pivot factors 7
RAND classifies superintelligence strategies into seven archetypes, each with a 'pathology': dominance (power concentration and value lock-in), co-development (founders' values become default), preparedness (normalising accumulated damage), moratorium (global surveillance), deterrence (eternal standoff), continuity of society (humanity survives as a relic), and acceleration (unpriced harms and dependence).
framework🗣 Matt Chessenconviction: highRAND
So what: A shared vocabulary for decoding which strategy policymakers and labs are implicitly pursuing.
The strategy choice hinges on five pivot questions: is danger close, is coexistence feasible, is restraint feasible, is a decisive strategic advantage reachable, and is suppression feasible; e.g., believing danger is far implies acceleration, while danger close plus infeasible coexistence plus feasible restraint implies a moratorium.
framework🗣 Matt Chessenconviction: highRAND
So what: Tracking how officials answer these five questions is a leading indicator of US AI policy direction.
“The first question it asks is, is danger close?” ▶ 16:46

HBS professor Randy Cohen (co-founder, PEO Partners) argues LBOs are structurally forced to buy companies matching all five Fama-French factors (high profitability, high payout, low multiple, low risk, small size), so a public portfolio of ~200 matched stocks with ~0.3-0.4x extra leverage and a put-spread-style hedge can replicate PE returns while charging ~100bp versus PE's 700+bp, enabling a 60/40 to 50/30/20 shift. He also covers market puzzles (momentum's -120% 2009 crash, ticker-confusion anomalies like CUBA and MCI), new inefficient markets as the source of durable alpha, and LLMs like Claude transforming finance research.

Cohen argues an LBO is economically forced to target companies with high profitability, high payout, low multiple, low risk and small size — exactly the five Fama-French factors — because paying 9–12% interest on roughly two-thirds debt means servicing 6–8% of enterprise value in cash annually.

Dwarkesh Podcast 1 episode(s) · 24 insights

What Robert Caro learned about power after studying it for 50 years61 min24 insights2026-10-30
▶ Watch on YouTube
Biographer Robert Caro discusses with Dwarkesh Patel how Robert Moses and Lyndon Johnson accumulated and used power: Moses overcame 1920s-era 'nothing can be built' obstacles through will, interlocking authorities and ruthlessness (later hardening into evictions like the Cross Bronx Expressway), while Johnson's persuasion was backed by leverage over what senators wanted. It is a history/biography conversation with no market content; relevant takeaways are about state capacity to build, the role of cheap Depression-era labor, and how power concentrates and decays.
State capacity and the 'can't build' debate · 6Cheap labor and the Depression advantage · 2Mechanics of Moses's power · 6Johnson: leverage behind persuasion · 6Research and writing method · 4
State capacity and the 'can't build' debate 6
Dwarkesh Patel cites New York's Second Avenue subway as having taken about 50 years to open a mile and a half at a cost of more than $4 billion, and California spending roughly $15 billion over a decade without a single new mile of rail.
data_point🗣 Dwarkesh Patelconviction: mediumSecond Avenue subwayCaliforniaNew York
So what: Illustrates the U.S. infrastructure cost-and-delay problem that frames the 'abundance' debate.
Caro rejects the idea that today's environmental, land-use and litigation safeguards make a Moses impossible, noting that in the 1920s people also said government could not build roads because property owners blocked them, and Moses built anyway.
contrarian🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highRobert MosesNew York
So what: Caro sees building paralysis as a leadership/political-genius gap more than a purely procedural one.
Caro argues that large-scale building periodically stalls for decades until a political genius appears who can get big public things built, citing Moses with public works and Johnson with civil rights.
framework🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highRobert MosesLyndon Johnson
So what: Infrastructure acceleration may depend on individual operators rather than policy reform alone.
“That’s the nature of political genius.” ▶ 11:20
Patel compares today's China to New York in the 1940s–50s, with a Moses-like attitude that built tens of thousands of miles of railways over 10–20 years at the cost of displacement and recklessness; Caro says he is not sure there is a good middle ground between the extremes.
framework🗣 Dwarkesh Patel / Robert Caroconviction: mediumChinaRobert Moses
So what: Trade-off between build speed and individual property rights may not be resolvable cleanly.
“I’m not sure there is a good spot.” ▶ 9:42
Caro says he does not want someone as ruthless and disregarding of public opinion as Moses, but that society needs someone who will find a way to get things built despite opposition — effectively agreeing 'we need a little Moses'.
thesis🗣 Robert Caroconviction: mediumRobert Moses
So what: Notable nuance from the author of the book credited with inspiring anti-Moses safeguards.
Caro says people who believe The Power Broker argues everything Moses did was bad 'didn't read the book', since hundreds of pages cover a young idealist reforming civil service toward merit promotion and opening Long Island beaches to city residents.
contrarian🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highRobert MosesThe Power BrokerJones Beach
So what: The canonical anti-Moses reading is an oversimplification by its own author's account.
Cheap labor and the Depression advantage 2
Caro agrees the Great Depression played a big role in Moses's early achievements, because thousands of out-of-work architects and laborers were available at very low wages and could be hired and fired ruthlessly since they had no other jobs.
causal🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highRobert MosesGreat Depression
So what: Public-works speed was partly a function of slack labor markets, a condition absent in tight labor markets today.
Caro explains that pre-war New York buildings had ornate stonework even on upper floors nobody could see because builders could hire skilled artisans at very low wages — 'people came cheap'.
causal🗣 Robert Caroconviction: mediumNew York
So what: Architectural quality decline is tied to rising relative cost of skilled craft labor (a Baumol-type effect).
Mechanics of Moses's power 6
Moses held interlocking posts — chairman of the State Power Authority and Triborough Bridge Authority, Parks Commissioner, Long Island Parks Commissioner, Jones Beach Commissioner — with differently ending terms, making him practically impossible to fire for decades, alongside his popularity.
framework🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highRobert MosesTriborough Bridge AuthorityState Power Authority
So what: Entrenched power is built through overlapping institutional positions that no single principal can revoke.
When Moses in 1962 used his long-standing tactic of threatening resignation, Governor Nelson Rockefeller simply accepted it; Caro says earlier mayors and governors technically could have done the same but faced overwhelming political cost until cracks appeared in his armor with age.
anecdote🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highRobert MosesNelson Rockefeller
So what: Leverage based on threatened exit works until a principal is willing to call the bluff.
Caro describes Moses hardening from idealist into someone who would build regardless of opposition, evicting tens of thousands without relocation provisions for the Cross Bronx Expressway, which became 'the world's longest traffic jam' the day it opened.
causal🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highRobert MosesCross Bronx Expressway
So what: Unchecked power degrades decision quality even in a once-effective builder.
When Bronx politician Henry Epstein proposed shifting the Cross Bronx Expressway two blocks south to evict a couple hundred rather than tens of thousands, Moses set out to destroy him by making his affair known; Caro says Moses learned to exploit weaknesses after failing to get things done when young.
anecdote🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highRobert MosesHenry EpsteinCross Bronx Expressway
So what: Power tactics included coercion via personal leverage.
“If he has a weakness, he’s going to use it.” ▶ 27:22
Caro recalls that when Moses was in power his secretary arrived after each interview with a list of callers wanting favors, but by the last interview there were no calls — a signal of lost power that Moses himself, insulated and in his 80s, never really recognized.
anecdote🗣 Robert Caroconviction: mediumRobert Moses
So what: Inbound demand for favors is a real-time gauge of power.
Caro says the one question he would ask Moses in an eighth interview is 'Did you realize you were changing?', and believes Moses did not.
anecdote🗣 Robert Caroconviction: mediumRobert Moses
So what: Self-awareness erodes as power accumulates.
Johnson: leverage behind persuasion 6
Caro says Johnson's famed persuasion was backed by power: senators knew he could grant or deny committee assignments and the passage of laws they wanted, so the arm-around-the-shoulder treatment carried implicit leverage.
framework🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highLyndon JohnsonU.S. Senate
So what: Influence is persuasion plus control of what the counterparty needs.
“Behind his persuasion was the power.” ▶ 33:30
Johnson controlled campaign money through John Connally, sometimes annotating requests with amounts or 'No, never', which meant that congressman would never get money from him.
anecdote🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highLyndon JohnsonJohn Connally
So what: Control of money flows was a core instrument of Johnson's political power.
Caro argues that had Johnson stayed majority leader under Kennedy, the 1963–65 civil rights and anti-poverty laws would not simply have happened earlier, because Kennedy, though charming and better at foreign policy, lacked Johnson's overriding desire to change America.
contrarian🗣 Robert Caroconviction: highLyndon JohnsonJohn F. Kennedy
So what: Legislative outcomes depended on the executive's drive, not just congressional mechanics.
Caro says Johnson's domestic agenda was derailed when his attention turned to Vietnam, which he calls the great tragedy of Johnson; he is still working out why Johnson kept escalating.
thesis🗣 Robert Caroconviction: mediumLyndon JohnsonVietnam
So what: Foreign entanglement crowded out domestic policy capacity.
“That’s the great tragedy of Johnson and Vietnam.” ▶ 38:59
Caro attributes Johnson's and Moses's 16-hour workdays to will rather than different physical constitutions, citing a senator Johnson called at 5 AM who replied he was 'just lying here waiting for your call'.
anecdote🗣 Robert Caroconviction: mediumLyndon JohnsonRobert Moses
So what: Relentless effort ('do everything') was the operating method of both.
Caro says he wishes Coke Stevenson had won the 1948 Senate election, judging him an idealist who knew how to get things done, and that Stevenson did not grasp what Johnson was willing to do to win.

Research and writing method 4
Before starting a book, Caro forces himself to reduce what the book is about to one sentence or at most a paragraph, a lesson learned the hard way after not doing it for The Power Broker.
